newsitem.title: USA: Adultery trial may embarrass U.S. Air Force-lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Adultery trial may embarrass U.S. Air Force-lawyer.

text.p: A court-martial trial for a woman bomber pilot would prove embarrassing to the U.S. Air Force but could be avoided if she were given an honourable discharge, her lawyer said on Monday.

Lawyer Frank Spinner told CNN that he would file a formal request later on Monday asking the Air Force to allow First Lieut. Kelly Flinn, the first female B-52 pilot, to resign with an honourable discharge.

"We'll be submitting the letter to the wing commander later this afternoon," Spinner told CNN from Minot, North Dakota, where Flinn's trial on adultery and other charges was scheduled to begin on Tuesday.

"We are going to argue that an honourable discharge in comparison with other cases is not an unreasonable outcome to this case. We are also going to argue that there are going to be many facts that will come out in a trial that will prove embarrassing to the Air Force," Spinner said, without elaborating.
Spinner has asked for a delay in the trial until June 2, but said the Pentagon had argued against a postponement. Arguments on a delay would be heard on Tuesday.

"It seems reasonable to allow the Secretary of the Air Force to resolve this issue and then if they want to go to trial we can go to trial," Spinner said. "Let's pull back, both sides now, let's reflect on this and see if we can come to a reasonable outcome for both sides."

It was unclear how quickly the Air Force chain of command could process Flinn's request, but the decision on whether to grant the honourable discharge would likely fall to Air Force Secretary Sheila Widnall.
Flinn has said she would rather go to trial than accept a less-than-honourable discharge, which Spinner said would preclude her from flying military planes for the National Guard.

Defence Secretary William Cohen, who would not comment directly on Flinn's case, said on Sunday it would be appropriate for the U.S. armed services to review their policies against fraternisation to ensure no sexual bias exists.
"I think a review of the regulations pertaining to whether there is uniformity throughout the services would be in order, but that's something for the services to conduct," Cohen said on CBS.
Flinn, 26 and single, has acknowledged having had an affair with a married civilian and is also accused of having sex with a lower-ranking enlisted man. She is also accused of lying.

Conviction of adultery in a military trial is punishable by penalties ranging up to dishonourable discharge and possible fines and imprisonment. Critics have argued that Flinn's case highlights a double standard in the way the U.S. Armed Forces treats the issue of adultery among its male and female staff.
